name: Holden
headline: Old mill villages and open hills,
just over the line from Worcester.
answer: Holden is a town of 19,905 people (2020 Census) in Worcester County, set in rolling hills on Worcester's northwest border. Its houses range from 1800s mill-village homes to suburban streets that grew after World War II. Routes 122A, 31 and 68 cross the town, and the commuter rail stops at Worcester station next door.
overview: Holden covers about thirty-six square miles of rolling upland northwest of Worcester, and the town notes that a good portion of that land is protected open space, watershed and recreation area. Settlement began around 1723, and Holden was incorporated on January 9, 1741, from what had been the north half of Worcester. Through the 1800s, textile mills grew up in villages such as Chaffin, Springdale, Dawsonville and Jefferson, northwest of the center, which remained the town's largest village until the early 1900s.

The landscape shifted again after 1900: building the Wachusett Reservoir (1900 to 1905) removed several mills, Worcester took large tracts as reservoir and watershed land, and most of the mills declined. After World War II, Holden became largely residential. Holden Center is still the civic heart along Main Street, where the Gale Free Library has used the Damon Memorial building since 1888. For time outside, the 660-acre Trout Brook Recreation Area and the town beach at Eagle Lake are within town lines, and the Mass Central Rail Trail follows the Quinapoxet River into Holden from Oakdale in West Boylston.

Housing policy in Holden has centered on the state's MBTA Communities law, which requires the town to zone for at least 750 multifamily units by right on at least 50 acres, at 15 or more units per acre. After a lawsuit brought on behalf of the Central Massachusetts Housing Alliance, the town submitted an action plan to the state in February 2025, but Town Meeting rejected a three-area rezoning that May. On January 29, 2026, the Attorney General sued Holden and eight other communities for noncompliance. A second plan, with overlay districts on the 39-acre Trap Rock quarry site at 2077 Main Street and 11.5 acres on Newbury Drive (an estimated 759 units in all), failed 520 to 257 at a Special Town Meeting on March 2, 2026. Holden is not on the state's list of compliant communities as of October 21, 2026.

housing.text: The Massachusetts Historical Commission's survey of Holden records one-story center-chimney Federal houses, mid-1800s side-passage houses with Greek Revival or Italianate trim, company tenements in Jefferson, and Bungalow and Four Square houses from 1915 to 1940, with suburban growth tied to Worcester after the 1920s. The town notes further residential growth after World War II. The 2020 Census counted 7,439 housing units in Holden. Much of the town is closed to building: Worcester came to control 3,332 acres in Holden as reservoir and watershed land, and the town's 2012 Open Space and Recreation Plan put about 30% of the town in permanently preserved open space.

villages.name: Holden Center
villages.line: The civic center of town, where houses have been built along Main Street since the 1790s.

villages.name: Jefferson
villages.line: The former industrial village northwest of the center, on the road to Rutland, where the Jefferson Manufacturing Co. owned 46 tenements in 1892.

villages.name: Eagleville
villages.line: A mill village between Holden Center and Jefferson, where a textile complex known as "Brick City" grew in the 1830s.

villages.name: Chaffin
villages.line: One of the villages that grew up around Holden's 19th-century mills.

villages.name: Dawsonville
villages.line: A former textile mill village; the Metropolitan District Commission demolished its mill in 1926.

commute.text: Holden has no commuter rail station of its own. The nearest MBTA stations are Worcester, on the Framingham/Worcester Line in the neighboring city, and Wachusett, the end of the Fitchburg Line, in Fitchburg.

places.name: Trout Brook Recreation Area
places.line: 660 acres of town conservation land with trails for walking, cross-country skiing and mountain biking, a pond, a picnic pavilion and a rentable lodge.

places.name: Eagle Lake
places.line: A town lake with a lifeguarded municipal beach, fishing and room for canoes and other non-motorized boats.

places.name: Mass Central Rail Trail
places.line: Stone-dust trail sections run about three miles along the Quinapoxet River from Oakdale in West Boylston to River Street, plus a 2.2-mile connector from River Street to Manning and Mill Streets.

places.name: Gale Free Library
places.line: The town library in the Damon Memorial building, dedicated in 1888, with a Local History Room.

places.name: Dawson Recreation Area
places.line: A town recreation site with a playground and baseball field, with expansion planned at 18 Industrial Drive.

places.name: Poutwater Pond Nature Preserve
places.line: State land around a rare acidic bog with a boardwalk, established in 1998 as the first nature preserve in Massachusetts, according to the town's open space plan.

places.name: Park Avenue Burying Ground
places.line: A cemetery laid out in 1826, which the town's open space plan describes as a prominent Federal-period landscape.

history.text: First European settlement, near a lime quarry in the southeast of present-day Holden.
Incorporated on January 9 from the north half of Worcester.
The east-west Massachusetts Central Railroad opened across the northern half of town.
The Worcester-Holden electric street railway began service.
Joined the first regional school district in Massachusetts.

search_notes: For 'Holden MA real estate agent', results are dominated by agent directories (HomeLight, Ramsey Solutions, Experience.com), Redfin filter pages, and Compass agent pages that match only because the agent's first name is Holden. 'Moving to Holden MA' returns Redfin's housing-market page and mover marketplaces (MoveBuddha, HireAHelper, uShip). No local guide explains the villages, the reservoir history or how Holden connects to Worcester, which is the gap a sourced community page can fill.

faq.q: What is the median home price in Holden, MA?
faq.a: The median single-family sale price in Holden was $550,000 in calendar year 2025, unchanged from 2024, across 200 sales (174 in 2024), according to The Warren Group's MA December 2025 Sales, Prices by Town report.
Not within town lines. The nearest MBTA stations are Worcester, on the Framingham/Worcester Line in neighboring Worcester, and Wachusett, the end of the Fitchburg Line, in Fitchburg.
Holden is part of the Wachusett Regional School District. Review its profile with DESE.

faq.q: What is the property tax rate in Holden, MA?
faq.a: Holden's FY2026 tax rate is $13.48 per $1,000 of assessed value, according to the town assessor's page, which lists a single rate for all property.

faq.q: Has Holden adopted MBTA Communities zoning?
faq.a: No. Town Meeting rejected rezoning plans in May 2025 and again on March 2, 2026, by 520 to 257, and the Attorney General sued the town for noncompliance in January 2026. Holden is not on the state's list of compliant communities as of October 21, 2026.

Fact-check 2026-10-22 (independent): Verified: population 19,905 and 7,439 housing units (Wikipedia); 36 square miles, January 9, 1741 incorporation, mill villages, post-war growth and 1954 regional district (town history page); MHC report facts (settlement ca. 1723 at the lime quarry, 1886 railroad, 1903 street railway, 3,332 acres, routes, house types, Dawsonville mill 1926); Trout Brook, Eagle Lake, Mass Central Rail Trail, Gale Free Library (dedicated August 29, 1888), Dawson Recreation Area, Poutwater Pond, Park Avenue Burying Ground and 30% preserved open space (2012 OSRP); FY2026 single rate $13.48 (assessor). MBTA Communities timeline verified: action plan submitted to EOHLC on Tuesday, February 25, 2025, after the Lawyers for Civil Rights suit in the name of CMHA (Banker & Tradesman, Feb 26, 2025); Article 37 rejected at the May 19, 2025 Annual Town Meeting, a three-area plan (Boston.com; Yahoo); AG suit against nine communities including Holden, January 29, 2026 (mass.gov); Article 2 failed 520 to 257 at the Special Town Meeting on March 2, 2026, with 750 units on 50 acres at 15 per acre required and two districts totaling an estimated 759 units (Boston.com; GBH confirms the date and a more than two-to-one margin); Holden absent from the compliance list as of October 21, 2026. A Yahoo preview had scheduled that meeting for February 23, 2026 and named the second site as the Halstead Apartments area; Boston.com, reporting the result, gives March 2 and Newbury Drive, which are kept. Corrected: Holden lies northwest of Worcester (Wikipedia: Worcester is to the southeast), not 'just north'; Jefferson is northwest of the center on the road to Rutland, not in the south of town, and Eagleville lies between the center and Jefferson (MHC report); the quarry at 2077 Main Street is described by Boston.com as effectively an active quarry (Trap Rock), so 'former' was removed; the reservoir sentence now follows the MHC report (Wachusett Reservoir 1900 to 1905 removed several mills) and the town page (most mills declined); Jefferson's 'dozens of tenements' is now the MHC figure, 46 in 1892. Removed: Holden Center 'on the central upland' (the MHC report calls the town an upland community but does not place the center); Jefferson's ZIP code (not in the cited source).
